# "SymplecticPartitionedRungeKutta" Method for NDSolve > Available Methods > Default Methods

The following table lists the current default choice of SPRK methods.

|       |               |                                                                          |           |      |
| ----- | ------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------ | --------- | ---- |
| Order | f evaluations | Method                                                                   | Symmetric | FSAL |
| 1     | 1             | Symplectic Euler                                                         | No        | No   |
| 2     | 1             | Symplectic pseudo Leapfrog                                               | Yes       | Yes  |
| 3     | 3             | McLachlan and Atela [[MA92](https://reference.wolfram.com/language/tutorial/NDSolveReferences#8579)]     | No        | No   |
| 4     | 5             | Suzuki [[S90](https://reference.wolfram.com/language/tutorial/NDSolveReferences#3309)]                   | Yes       | Yes  |
| 6     | 11            | Sofroniou and Spaletta [[SS05](https://reference.wolfram.com/language/tutorial/NDSolveReferences#17586)] | Yes       | Yes  |
| 8     | 19            | Sofroniou and Spaletta [[SS05](https://reference.wolfram.com/language/tutorial/NDSolveReferences#17586)] | Yes       | Yes  |
| 10    | 35            | Sofroniou and Spaletta [[SS05](https://reference.wolfram.com/language/tutorial/NDSolveReferences#17586)] | Yes       | Yes  |

Unlike the situation for explicit Runge–Kutta methods, the coefficients for high-order SPRK methods are only given numerically in the literature. Yoshida [[Y90](https://reference.wolfram.com/language/tutorial/NDSolveReferences#21389)] only gives coefficients accurate to 14 decimal digits of accuracy for example.

Since ``NDSolve`` also works for arbitrary precision, you need a process for obtaining the coefficients to the same precision as that to be used in the solver.

When the closed form of the coefficients is not available, the order equations for the symmetric composition coefficients can be refined in arbitrary precision using ``FindRoot``, starting from the known machine-precision solution.

</result>

<result url='https://reference.wolfram.com/language/tutorial/NDSolvePackages#2134588770'>

# Utility Packages for Numerical Differential Equation Solving > NDSolveUtilities

A number of utility routines have been written to facilitate the investigation and comparison of various ``NDSolve`` methods. These functions have been collected in the package ``DifferentialEquations`NDSolveUtilities```.

|     |     |
| --- | --- |
| CompareMethods[sys, refsol, methods, opts] | return statistics for various methods applied to the system sys |
| FinalSolutions[sys, sols] | return the solution values at the end of the numerical integration for various solutions sols corresponding to the system sys |
| InvariantErrorPlot[invts, dvars, ivar, sol, opts] | return a plot of the error in the invariants invts for the solution sol |
| RungeKuttaLinearStabilityFunction[amat, bvec, var] | return the linear stability function for the Runge–Kutta method with coefficient matrix amat and weight vector bvec using the variable var |
| StepDataPlot[sols, opts] | return plots of the step sizes taken for the solutions sols on a logarithmic scale |

Functions provided in the ``NDSolveUtilities`` package.

This loads the package:

```wl
In[1]:= Needs["DifferentialEquations`NDSolveUtilities`"]
```

A useful means of analyzing Runge–Kutta methods is to study how they behave when applied to a scalar linear test problem (see the package ``FunctionApproximations.m``).

This assigns the (exact or infinitely precise) coefficients for the 2-stage implicit Runge–Kutta Gauss method of order 4:

```wl
In[2]:= {amat, bvec, cvec}  = NDSolve`ImplicitRungeKuttaGaussCoefficients[4, Infinity]

Out[2]= {{{(1/4), (1/12) (3 - 2 Sqrt[3])}, {(1/12) (3 + 2 Sqrt[3]), (1/4)}}, {(1/2), (1/2)}, {(1/6) (3 - Sqrt[3]), (1/6) (3 + Sqrt[3])}}
```

This computes the linear stability function, which corresponds to the (2,2) Padé approximation to the exponential at the origin:

```wl
In[3]:= RungeKuttaLinearStabilityFunction[amat, bvec, z]

Out[3]= (1 + (z/2) + (z^2/12)/1 - (z/2) + (z^2/12))
```

Examples of the functions ``CompareMethods``, ``FinalSolutions``, ``RungeKuttaLinearStabilityFunction``, and ``StepDataPlot`` can be found within ["ExplicitRungeKutta Method for NDSolve"](https://reference.wolfram.com/language/tutorial/NDSolveExplicitRungeKutta).

Examples of the function ``InvariantErrorPlot`` can be found within ["Projection Method for NDSolve"](https://reference.wolfram.com/language/tutorial/NDSolveProjection).

</result>

<result url='https://reference.wolfram.com/language/tutorial/NDSolveExtrapolation#1938414111'>

# "Extrapolation" Method for NDSolve > Introduction

Extrapolation methods are a class of arbitrary-order methods with automatic order and step-size control. The error estimate comes from computing a solution over an interval using the same method with a varying number of steps and using extrapolation on the polynomial that fits through the computed solutions, giving a composite higher-order method [[BS64](https://reference.wolfram.com/language/tutorial/NDSolveReferences#22705)]. At the same time, the polynomials give a means of error estimation.

Typically, for low precision, the extrapolation methods have not been competitive with Runge–Kutta-type methods. For high precision, however, the arbitrary order means that they can be arbitrarily faster than fixed-order methods for very precise tolerances.

The order and step-size control are based on the codes ``odex.f`` and ``seulex.f`` described in [[HNW93](https://reference.wolfram.com/language/tutorial/NDSolveReferences#24148)] and [[HW96](https://reference.wolfram.com/language/tutorial/NDSolveReferences#32197)].

This loads packages that contain some utility functions for plotting step sequences and some predefined problems:

```wl
In[1]:=
Needs["DifferentialEquations`NDSolveProblems`"];
Needs["DifferentialEquations`NDSolveUtilities`"];
```

</result>

<result url='https://reference.wolfram.com/language/tutorial/NDSolveExplicitRungeKutta#942526595'>

# "ExplicitRungeKutta" Method for NDSolve > Coefficient Plug-in > ode23

This defines the coefficients for a 3(2) FSAL explicit Runge–Kutta pair.

The third-order formula is due to Ralston, and the embedded method was derived by Bogacki and Shampine [[BS89a](https://reference.wolfram.com/language/tutorial/NDSolveReferences#2609)].

This defines a function for computing the coefficients to a desired precision:

```wl
In[1]:=
BSamat = {{1 / 2}, {0, 3 / 4}, {2 / 9, 1 / 3, 4 / 9}};
BSbvec = {2 / 9, 1 / 3, 4 / 9, 0};
BScvec = {1 / 2, 3 / 4, 1};
BSevec = {-5 / 72, 1 / 12, 1 / 9, -1 / 8};
BSCoefficients[4, p_] := 
	N[{BSamat, BSbvec, BScvec, BSevec}, p];
```

The method is used in the Texas Instruments TI-85 pocket calculator, Matlab, and RKSUITE [[S94](https://reference.wolfram.com/language/tutorial/NDSolveReferences#94091990)]. Unfortunately it does not allow for the form of stiffness detection that has been chosen.

</result>

<result url='https://reference.wolfram.com/language/tutorial/NDSolveExplicitRungeKutta#863097980'>

# "ExplicitRungeKutta" Method for NDSolve > Coefficient Plug-in > A Dormand–Prince Method

Here is how to define a 5(4) pair of Dormand and Prince coefficients [[DP80](https://reference.wolfram.com/language/tutorial/NDSolveReferences#20618)]. This is currently the method used by ``ode45`` in Matlab.

This defines a function for computing the coefficients to a desired precision:

```wl
In[1]:=
DOPRIamat = {
	{1 / 5}, 
	{3 / 40, 9 / 40}, 
	{44 / 45, -56 / 15, 32 / 9}, 
	{19372 / 6561, -25360 / 2187, 64448 / 6561, -212 / 729}, 
	{9017 / 3168, -355 / 33, 46732 / 5247, 49 / 176, -5103 / 18656}, 
	{35 / 384, 0, 500 / 1113, 125 / 192, -2187 / 6784, 11 / 84}};
DOPRIbvec = {35 / 384, 0, 500 / 1113, 125 / 192, -2187 / 6784, 11 / 84, 0};
DOPRIcvec = {1 / 5, 3 / 10, 4 / 5, 8 / 9, 1, 1};
DOPRIevec = {71 / 57600, 0, -71 / 16695, 71 / 1920, -17253 / 339200, 22 / 525, -1 / 40};
DOPRICoefficients[5, p_] := 
	N[{DOPRIamat, DOPRIbvec, DOPRIcvec, DOPRIevec}, p];
```

The Dormand–Prince method is a FSAL scheme since the coefficient matrix is of the form (\!\(\*CounterBox["NumberedEquation", "FSALButcherTable"]\)); it is a seven-stage scheme, but effectively uses only six function evaluations.

Here is how the coefficients of Dormand and Prince can be used in place of the built-in choice. Since the structure of the coefficients includes an error vector, the implementation is able to ascertain that adaptive step sizes can be computed:

```wl
In[2]:= NDSolve[system, Method -> {"ExplicitRungeKutta", "DifferenceOrder" -> 5, "Coefficients" -> DOPRICoefficients, "StiffnessTest" -> False}]

Out[2]= {{Subscript[Y, 1][T] -> InterpolatingFunction[{{0., 20.}}, <>][T], Subscript[Y, 2][T] -> InterpolatingFunction[{{0., 20.}}, <>][T]}}
```

</result>

<result url='https://reference.wolfram.com/language/tutorial/NDSolveExplicitRungeKutta#494313012'>

# "ExplicitRungeKutta" Method for NDSolve > Method Plug-in

This shows how to implement the classical explicit Runge–Kutta method of order four using the method plug-in environment.

This definition is optional since the method in fact has no data. However, any expression can be stored inside the data object. For example, the coefficients could be approximated here to avoid coercion from rational to floating-point numbers at each integration step:

```wl
In[1]:= ClassicalRungeKutta/:NDSolve`InitializeMethod[ClassicalRungeKutta, __] := ClassicalRungeKutta[];
```

The actual method implementation is written using a stepping procedure:

```wl
In[2]:=
ClassicalRungeKutta[___]["Step"[f_, t_, h_, y_, yp_]] := Block[{deltay, k1, k2, k3, k4}, 
	k1 = yp;
	k2 = f[t + 1 / 2 h, y + 1 / 2 h k1];
	k3 = f[t + 1 / 2 h, y + 1 / 2 h k2];
	k4 = f[t + h, y + h k3];
	deltay = h (1 / 6 k1 + 1 / 3 k2 + 1 / 3 k3 + 1 / 6 k4);
	{h, deltay}
	];
```

Notice that the implementation closely resembles the description that you might find in a textbook. There are no memory allocation/deallocation statements or type declarations, for example. In fact the implementation works for machine real numbers or machine complex numbers, and even using arbitrary-precision software arithmetic.

Here is an example of the calling syntax. For simplicity the method only uses fixed step sizes, so you need to specify what step sizes to take:

```wl
In[3]:= NDSolve[system, Method -> ClassicalRungeKutta, StartingStepSize -> 1 / 10]

Out[3]= {{Subscript[Y, 1][T] -> InterpolatingFunction[{{0., 20.}}, <>][T], Subscript[Y, 2][T] -> InterpolatingFunction[{{0., 20.}}, <>][T]}}
```

Many of the methods that have been built into ``NDSolve`` were first prototyped using top-level code before being implemented in the kernel for efficiency.

</result>

<result url='https://reference.wolfram.com/language/tutorial/NDSolveExplicitRungeKutta#364415127'>

# "ExplicitRungeKutta" Method for NDSolve > Coefficient Plug-in

The implementation of ``"ExplicitRungeKutta"`` provides a default method pair at each order.

Sometimes, however, it is convenient to use a different method, for example:

* To replicate the results of someone else.

* To use a special-purpose method that works well for a specific problem.

* To experiment with a new method.

</result>

<result url='https://reference.wolfram.com/language/tutorial/NDSolveExplicitRungeKutta#308103003'>

# "ExplicitRungeKutta" Method for NDSolve > Option Summary

|     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- |
| option name | default value |     |
| "Coefficients" | EmbeddedExplicitRungeKuttaCoefficients | specify the coefficients of the explicit Runge–Kutta method |
| "DifferenceOrder" | Automatic | specify the order of local accuracy |
| "EmbeddedDifferenceOrder" | Automatic | specify the order of the embedded method in a pair of explicit Runge–Kutta methods |
| "StepSizeControlParameters" | Automatic | specify the PI step-control parameters (see (\!\(\*CounterBox["NumberedEquation", "PIController"]\))) |
| "StepSizeRatioBounds" | {(1/8), 4} | specify the bounds on a relative change in the new step size (see (\!\(\*CounterBox["NumberedEquation", "StepSizeRatioBounds"]\))) |
| "StepSizeSafetyFactors" | Automatic | specify the safety factors to use in the step-size estimate (see (\!\(\*CounterBox["NumberedEquation", "StepSizeSafetyFactors"]\))) |
| "StiffnessTest" | Automatic | specify whether to use the stiffness detection capability |

Options of the method ``"ExplicitRungeKutta"``.

The default setting of ``Automatic`` for the option ``"DifferenceOrder"`` selects the default coefficient order based on the problem, initial values, and local error tolerances, balanced against the work of the method for each coefficient set.

The default setting of ``Automatic`` for the option ``"EmbeddedDifferenceOrder"`` specifies that the default order of the embedded method is one lower than the method order. This depends on the value of the ``"DifferenceOrder"`` option.

The default setting of ``Automatic`` for the option ``"StepSizeControlParameters"`` uses the values ``{1, 0}`` if stiffness detection is active and ``{3 / 10, 2 / 5}`` otherwise.

The default setting of ``Automatic`` for the option ``"StepSizeSafetyFactors"`` uses the values ``{17 / 20, 9 / 10}`` if the I step controller (\!\(\*CounterBox["NumberedEquation", "IController"]\)) is used and ``{9 / 10, 9 / 10}`` if the PI step controller (\!\(\*CounterBox["NumberedEquation", "PIController"]\)) is used. The step controller used depends on the values of the options ``"StepSizeControlParameters"`` and ``"StiffnessTest"``.

The default setting of ``Automatic`` for the option ``"StiffnessTest"`` will activate the stiffness test if the coefficients have the form (\!\(\*CounterBox["NumberedEquation", "StiffButcherTable"]\)).

</result>

<result url='https://reference.wolfram.com/language/tutorial/NDSolveExplicitRungeKutta#2096253211'>

# "ExplicitRungeKutta" Method for NDSolve > Stiffness > Linear Stability

Consider applying a Runge–Kutta method to a linear scalar equation known as Dahlquist's equation:

```wl
y'(t)=λ y(t), λ∈\[DoubleStruckCapitalC], Re(λ) < 0.
```

The result is a rational function of polynomials R(z) where z=h λ (see for example [[L87](https://reference.wolfram.com/language/tutorial/NDSolveReferences#7030)]).

This utility function finds the linear stability function R(z) for Runge–Kutta methods. The form depends on the coefficients and is a polynomial if the Runge–Kutta method is explicit.

Here is the stability function for the fifth-order scheme in the Dormand–Prince 5(4) pair:

```wl
In[1]:= DOPRIsf = RungeKuttaLinearStabilityFunction[DOPRIamat, DOPRIbvec, z]

Out[1]= 1 + z + (z^2/2) + (z^3/6) + (z^4/24) + (z^5/120) + (z^6/600)
```

This function finds the linear stability function R(z) for Runge–Kutta methods. The form depends on the coefficients and is a polynomial if the Runge–Kutta method is explicit.

The following package is useful for visualizing linear stability regions for numerical methods for differential equations:

```wl
In[2]:= Needs["FunctionApproximations`"];
```

You can now visualize the absolute stability region |R(z)|=1 :

```wl
In[3]:= OrderStarPlot[DOPRIsf, 1, z]

Out[3]= <image removed>
```

Depending on the magnitude of λ in (\!\(\*CounterBox["NumberedEquation", "DahlquistEquation"]\)), if you choose the step size h such that |R(h λ)| < 1, then errors in successive steps will be damped, and the method is said to be absolutely stable.

If |R(h λ)| > 1, then step-size selection will be restricted by stability and not by local accuracy.

</result>

<result url='https://reference.wolfram.com/language/tutorial/NDSolveExplicitRungeKutta#1608101326'>

# "ExplicitRungeKutta" Method for NDSolve > Coefficient Plug-in > Method Comparison

Here you solve a system using several explicit Runge–Kutta pairs.

For the Fehlberg 4(5) pair, the option ``"EmbeddedDifferenceOrder"`` is used to specify the order of the embedded method:

```wl
In[1]:= Fehlberg45 = {"ExplicitRungeKutta", "Coefficients" -> FehlbergCoefficients, "DifferenceOrder" -> 4, "EmbeddedDifferenceOrder" -> 5, "StiffnessTest" -> False};
```

The Dormand and Prince 5(4) pair is defined as follows:

```wl
In[2]:= DOPRI54  = {"ExplicitRungeKutta", "Coefficients" -> DOPRICoefficients, "DifferenceOrder" -> 5, "StiffnessTest" -> False};
```

The 5(4) pair of Bogacki and Shampine is the default order-five method:

```wl
In[3]:= BS54  = {"ExplicitRungeKutta", "Coefficients" -> "EmbeddedExplicitRungeKuttaCoefficients", "DifferenceOrder" -> 5, "StiffnessTest" -> False};
```

Put the methods and some descriptive names together in a list:

```wl
In[4]:=
names = {"Fehlberg 4(5)", "Dormand-Prince 5(4)", "Bogacki-Shampine 5(4)"};

	
methods = {Fehlberg45, DOPRI54, BS54};
```

Compute the number of integration steps, function evaluations, and the endpoint global error:

```wl
In[5]:= data = CompareMethods[system, refsol, methods];
```

Display the results in a table:

```wl
In[6]:=
labels = {"Method", "Steps", "Cost", "Error"};
TabulateResults[labels, names, data]

Out[50]//DisplayForm=
|                         |           |      |                         |
| ----------------------- | --------- | ---- | ----------------------- |
| Method                  | Steps     | Cost | Error                   |
| Fehlberg 4(5)           | {306, 11} | 1893 | 2.0217259155685952`*^-7 |
| Dormand - Prince 5(4)   | {279, 10} | 1736 | 2.1220469992311308`*^-8 |
| Bogacki - Shampine 5(4) | {180, 16} | 1374 | 5.798895919006952`*^-9  |
```

The default method was the least expensive and provided the most accurate solution.

</result>

<result url='https://reference.wolfram.com/language/tutorial/NDSolveDesign#822488195'>

# The Design of the NDSolve Framework > Automatic Selection and User Controllability

The framework provides automatic step-size selection and method-order selection. Methods are user-configurable via method options.

For example, a user can select the class of ``"ExplicitRungeKutta"`` methods, and the code will automatically attempt to ascertain the "optimal" order according to the problem, the relative and absolute local error tolerances, and the initial step-size estimate.

Here is a list of options appropriate for ``"ExplicitRungeKutta"``.

```wl
In[1]:= Options[NDSolve`ExplicitRungeKutta]

Out[1]= {"Coefficients" -> "EmbeddedExplicitRungeKuttaCoefficients", "DifferenceOrder" -> Automatic, "EmbeddedDifferenceOrder" -> Automatic, "StepSizeControlParameters" -> Automatic, "StepSizeRatioBounds" -> {(1/8), 4}, "StepSizeSafetyFactors" -> Automatic, "StiffnessTest" -> Automatic}
```

</result>

<result url='https://reference.wolfram.com/language/tutorial/NDSolveDesign#81128075'>

# The Design of the NDSolve Framework > Some Basic Methods

|     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- |
| order | method | formula |
| 1   | Explicit Euler | yn + 1=yn + hnf(tn, yn) |
| 2   | Explicit Midpoint | yn + 1 / 2=yn + (hn/2)f(tn, yn) yn + 1=yn + hnf(tn + 1 / 2, yn + 1 / 2) |
| 1   | Backward or Implicit Euler (1-stage RadauIIA) | yn + 1=yn + hnf(tn + 1, yn + 1) |
| 2   | Implicit Midpoint (1-stage Gauss) | yn + 1=yn + hnf(tn + 1 / 2, (1/2)(yn + 1 + yn)) |
| 2   | Trapezoidal (2-stage Lobatto IIIA) | yn + 1=yn + (hn/2)(f(tn, yn) + f(tn + 1, yn + 1)) |
| 1   | Linearly Implicit Euler | (I - hnJ)(yn + 1 - yn)=hnf(tn, yn) |
| 2   | Linearly Implicit Midpoint | (I - (hn/2)J)(yn + 1 / 2 - yn)=(hn/2)f(tn, yn) (I - (hn/2)J)((Δ yn - Δ yn - 1 / 2)/2)=(hn/2)f(tn + 1 / 2, yn + 1 / 2) - Δ yn - 1 / 2 |

Some of the one-step methods that have been implemented.

Here Δ Subscript[y, n]=Subscript[y, n + 1] - Subscript[y, n + 1 / 2], I denotes the identity matrix, and J denotes the Jacobian matrix (∂f/∂y)(Subscript[t, n], Subscript[y, n]).

Although the implicit midpoint method has not been implemented as a separate method, it is available through the one-stage Gauss scheme of the ``"ImplicitRungeKutta"`` method.

</result>

<result url='https://reference.wolfram.com/language/tutorial/NDSolveDesign#618070850'>

# The Design of the NDSolve Framework > Method Classes

Methods such as ``"ExplicitRungeKutta"`` include a number of schemes of different orders. Moreover, alternative coefficient choices can be specified by the user. This is a generalization of the ideas found in RKSUITE [[BGS93](https://reference.wolfram.com/language/tutorial/NDSolveReferences#6300)].

</result>

<result url='https://reference.wolfram.com/language/tutorial/NDSolveDAE#1946837507'>

# Numerical Solution of Differential-Algebraic Equations > DAE Solution Methods

There are a variety of solution methods built into ``NDSolve`` for solving DAEs.

Two methods work with the general residual form of index-1 DAEs, F(t, x, Derivative[1][x])=0.

* [IDA—](https://reference.wolfram.com/language/tutorial/NDSolveIDAMethod)(Implicit Differential-Algebraic solver from the SUNDIALS package) based on backward differentiation formulas (BDF)

* [StateSpace—](https://reference.wolfram.com/language/tutorial/NDSolveStateSpace)implicitly solves F(t, x, Derivative[1][x])=0 for derivatives Derivative[1][x] to use an underlying ODE solver

If the system has index higher than 1, both of these solvers typically fail. To accurately solve such systems, index reduction is needed. Note that index-1 systems can be reduced to ODEs, but it is often more efficient to use one of the solvers above.

``NDSolve`` also has some solvers that work with DAEs that can be reduced to special forms.

* MassMatrix—for DAEs of the form M. Derivative[1][x](t)=f(t, x(t))

* [Projection—](https://reference.wolfram.com/language/tutorial/NDSolveProjection)for ODEs Derivative[1][x](t)=f(t, x(t)) with invariants g(t, x(t))=0

The following subsections describe some aspects of using these methods for DAEs.

</result>

<result url='https://reference.wolfram.com/language/ref/NDSolveValue#5349239'>

# NDSolveValue > Examples > Scope > Ordinary Differential Equations > 6

Define a Van der Pol equation:

```wl
In[1]:= vdp = {x'[t] == y[t], y'[t] == -x[t] + 1000(1 - x[t] ^ 2)y[t], x[0] == 2, y[0] == 0};
```

The solution's "stiff" behavior that the default solver automatically handles:

```wl
In[2]:= {xsol, ysol} = NDSolveValue[vdp, {x, y}, {t, 2000}]

Out[2]=
{InterpolatingFunction[{{0., 2000.}}, {5, 7, 1, {1827}, {4}, 0, 0, 0, 0, Automatic, {}, {}, False}, 
 CompressedData["«15987»"], {Developer`PackedArrayForm, 
  CompressedData["«3404»"], 
  CompressedData["«38324»"]}, {Automatic}], InterpolatingFunction[{{0., 2000.}}, {5, 7, 1, {1827}, {4}, 0, 0, 0, 0, Automatic, {}, {}, False}, 
 CompressedData["«15987»"], {Developer`PackedArrayForm, 
  CompressedData["«3404»"], 
  CompressedData["«39412»"]}, {Automatic}]}

In[3]:= Plot[Evaluate[xsol[t]], {t, 0, 2000}, PlotRange -> All]

Out[3]= <image removed>
```

Other methods may not be able to solve this system:

```wl
In[4]:= NDSolveValue[{Derivative[1][x][t] == y[t], Derivative[1][y][t] == -x[t] + 1000(1 - x[t]^2)y[t], x[0] == 2, y[0] == 0}, {x, y}, {t, 2000}, Method -> "ExplicitRungeKutta"]

Out[4]=
{InterpolatingFunction[{{0., 0.008522740924400746}}, {5, 7, 1, {12}, {4}, 0, 0, 0, 0, Automatic, {}, 
  {}, False}, {{0., 0.0004660296519799167, 0.0009320593039598334, 0.0014501741487707165, 
   0.0020771261484261176, 0.0026240294216901437, 0.00340 ... 33436, -0.000010674354819606435, -0.00066666808370892, 
   -9.6095002022345*^-7, -0.0006666685952113513, -4.1200298217525244*^-7, -0.0006666690833056001, 
   -3.7589435919471725*^-7, -0.0006666695759931179, -3.7142514042187713*^-7}}, {Automatic}]}
```
